title: Earthquakes
aka: the earthquake in the days of Uzziah
lead: The land of Israel lies along an active fault, and the Bible remembers its earthquakes, one so great that people still dated events by it centuries later. Quakes mark God's coming at Sinai and in the psalms, the death and resurrection of Jesus, Paul's release at Philippi, and the judgments of Revelation.

sections.b:
The Jordan valley, the Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee lie on the Dead Sea Transform, the boundary where the African and Arabian plates grind past each other, and the region has suffered many great earthquakes in recorded history. The Bible's best-remembered one dates the book of Amos, "two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1; Hebrew ha-ra'ash), in the reign of Uzziah. Zechariah, centuries later, still says, "You will run away just as you ran from the earthquake in the time of King Uzziah of Judah" (Zechariah 14:5). Josephus tells a later tradition that when Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense, "a great earthquake shook the ground and a rent was made in the temple," and the sun's rays fell on the king's face and he was struck with skin disease (Antiquities 9.10.4); 2 Chronicles 26:16–21 tells of the incense and the disease but says nothing of a quake. Josephus also reports a great earthquake in Judea in the seventh year of Herod, when "about ten thousand men also perished by the fall of houses" (Antiquities 15.5.2).

Other shakings in the story: the ground splits and swallows Korah's company (Numbers 16:31–33), and during Jonathan's raid "The ground itself quaked. It was a trembling from God" (1 Samuel 14:15).

sections.h: The earth shakes when God comes
sections.b: At Sinai "the whole mountain quaked hard" (Exodus 19:18). The psalms and prophets describe God's coming the same way: "The earth heaved and quaked" (Psalm 18:7; compare Judges 5:4–5; Psalm 68:8; Psalm 104:32; Psalm 114:4; Nahum 1:5; Isaiah 29:6). Ezekiel foresees "a great earthquake" in the land of Israel on the day of Gog (Ezekiel 38:19). Haggai's "I am about to shake the heavens and the earth" is taken up in Hebrews 12:26–27 (see The Shaking of the Heavens and the Earth). Yet when Elijah stood on the mountain, "The LORD was not in the quake" but came after it, in "a sound of thin silence" (1 Kings 19:11–12). For the believer the shaking is no cause for terror: "So we will have no fear when the earth changes place" (Psalm 46:2).

sections.h: In the Gospels, Acts and Revelation
sections.b:
Jesus lists "famines and earthquakes in place after place" among the troubles before the end (Matthew 24:7; Mark 13:8; Luke 21:11), but adds that "the end is not here yet" and that these are "only the start of the labor pains" (Matthew 24:6, 8). Only Matthew tells of the earthquakes at the cross and the tomb: when Jesus died, "The earth quaked and the rocks broke apart" and tombs were opened (Matthew 27:51–54), and on Easter morning "the ground shook hard" as the angel rolled the stone away (Matthew 28:2). The opened graves recall God's promise in Ezekiel: "Look, I am opening your graves" (Ezekiel 37:12).

In Acts the house where the believers prayed "shook" (Acts 4:31), and at Philippi "a strong earthquake struck" and the prison doors swung open (Acts 16:26). In Revelation earthquakes come with the sixth seal, before and after the trumpets, and at the seventh bowl (Revelation 6:12; Revelation 8:5; Revelation 11:13; Revelation 11:19), the last "one with no equal since people came to be on the earth" (Revelation 16:18).
